chapter_theme: A ruler's real enemy is his own faults: arrogance, anger, desire, avarice, misplaced pride and self-regard. Small ones must be treated as large and dealt with before they arrive, and only one who has cleared his own is fit to judge others.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: what the faults are (431-432), why they must be removed in general (433-436), then specific treatment: avarice (437-438), pride (439), and desire (440).

431.reading: The prosperity of those without arrogance, anger and smallness has a dignified quality.
431.nuance: The verse puts the virtue in the quality of the prosperity: the same wealth is dignified or not, depending on who holds it.

positions.position: செருக்கு is intoxication from wealth, and சிறுமை is excessive desire, which he calls small because it is what small people do.
செருக்கு is coveting another man's wife, and சிறுமை is any behaviour of petty people.
positions.quote: பிறர்மனை நயத்தலும், வெகுளியும், சிறியார் செய்வன செய் தொழுகுதலும்

432.reading: Stinginess, honour that has passed beyond dignity, and joy that lacks dignity are faults in a ruler.
432.nuance: The surprising items are positive feelings gone wrong. Parimelazhagar makes the undignified joy excessive leniency, கழிகண்ணோட்டம், and the wrong honour includes refusing to bow to elders and carrying a thing through just because one intended it.

433.reading: Though a fault comes as small as a millet seed, those who are ashamed of blame take it to be as large as a palmyra.
433.nuance: The motive is shame at blame, பழிநாணுவார், so this is social conscience. Parimelazhagar makes the scale practical: treating it as large is how they ensure it doesn't come again.

434.reading: Guard against fault itself as your aim; fault alone is the enemy that brings ruin.
434.nuance: The double ஏ, குற்றமே twice, refuses any other candidate. Parimelazhagar draws a strong conclusion from a Sanskrit view: external enemies can only bring ruin through such faults. பொருளாக is 'as your aim' for him; Pope's 'wealth' is a different and weaker reading.

435.reading: The life of one who doesn't guard before it comes will perish like straw set before a fire.

positions.position: What is coming is fault, supplied from the chapter's subject; even a small fault burns away great wealth.
positions.quote: குற்றம் வரக் கடவதாகின்ற முற்காலத்திலே அதனைக் காவாத அரசன் வாழ்க்கை

positions.position: What is coming is suffering, and failing to prepare against it is itself the fault.
positions.quote: இது முந்துற்றுக் காவல் செய்வன செய்யாமையும் குற்ற மென்றது.

436.reading: If he removes his own fault and can then see others' faults, what fault can attach to a ruler?
436.nuance: Parimelazhagar turns this into a condition of legitimacy: punishing others' faults is itself a fault until one has cleared one's own, after which it becomes justice. The verse's order, தன்... பிறர், supports him, though the claim about the right to judge is his.

437.reading: The wealth of one who clings to it, not doing what should be done with it, does not last but perishes.
437.nuance: Stinginess doesn't keep wealth, on this view; it loses it. Parimelazhagar's explanation is that wealth left unused for virtue and growth has nothing to sustain it.

438.reading: The miserliness called the clinging heart is not a thing to be counted among any.
438.nuance: பற்றுள்ளம் uses a word close to the attachment renunciation speaks of, here applied to wealth in the Porul section.

positions.position: It can't be counted among faults because it exceeds them all: it can dominate even when every good quality is present.
positions.quote: குற்றத் தன்மைகள் எல்லாவற்றுள்ளும் வைத்து எண்ணப்படுவது ஒன்று அன்று; மிக்கது.

positions.position: It isn't counted because it is contemptible: useless to self and others, it is reckoned as nothing.
positions.quote: இஃது உலோபம் தனக்கும் பிறர்க்கும் பயன்படாமையால் ஒரு பொருளாக மதிக்கப்படாதென்றது.

439.reading: Never admire yourself, and never set your heart on a deed that brings no good.
439.nuance: The two clauses could be separate, or the second a consequence of the first, as Manakkudavar and Kalaignar take it. Parimelazhagar connects them too: self-admiration blinds one to place, time and strength, the subjects of chapters 48 to 50.

440.reading: If you can enjoy what you love without others knowing of the love, your enemies' schemes come to nothing.
440.nuance: A striking end. After a chapter on removing faults, the last verse manages one by concealing it. Parimelazhagar concedes that desire, anger and joy aren't to be wholly removed. The verse is a matter of security: a known desire is a door for the enemy.

links.note: Millet and palmyra both times: 104 inflates a small favour received, and 433 a small fault committed. The same discipline of scale runs in both directions, gratitude for others and severity with oneself.
Same shape and the same காண்கிற்பின். 190 asks anyone to see their own faults as they see others', and 436 makes the order a condition for a ruler who judges.
384 requires மானம் of a king; 432 forbids மானம் that has passed beyond dignity. The same word marks a virtue and a fault, and Parimelazhagar explicitly separates them in both places.

431 praises those without desire, and 440 tells one how to enjoy desire safely. Parimelazhagar resolves this by making the fault excess in 431, but the verses themselves pull apart. Removing and hiding are different programmes.

source_issues: 437: The Manakkudavar entry is marked [#] and labelled as Parimelazhagar's commentary, and is close to it in wording. I did not use it as an independent view.
439: Parimelazhagar's gloss reads நான்கு மதியாது, probably a corruption of நன்கு.
439: Manakkudavar's பொய்யனாக நினைத்து is obscure and may be corrupt, so I did not rely on it.
